subject: english
name: English

pillars.name: Reading & Understanding
pillars.scope: The student misunderstands the text: what it says, what it means, its tone, purpose or devices.

pillars.name: Thesis & Organisation
pillars.scope: The reading may be right, but the argument or plan is wrong: off the prompt, no arguable thesis, drifting, badly ordered, wrong form.

pillars.name: Evidence & Analysis
pillars.scope: The thesis is sound, but proving it goes wrong: summary instead of analysis, missing, weak or unexplained evidence.

pillars.name: Grammar & Mechanics
pillars.scope: The ideas are sound; a sentence-level convention slips (sentence boundaries, agreement, tense, spelling, punctuation).

pillars.name: Style & Expression
pillars.scope: The ideas are sound, but how they are expressed gets in the way: unclear, informal, imprecise, repetitive, unlinked, or wrongly cited.

pillars.name: Task Habits
pillars.scope: How the student handles the task: blanks, unfinished work, missed parts, length, not rereading the text, not proofreading.

decision_order: Does the student misunderstand the text (CON)?
Is the reading right but the thesis, plan or form wrong (STR)?
Is the thesis right but the evidence or analysis weak (PRC)?
Is it a sentence-level grammar or mechanics slip (FAC)?
Are the ideas right but expressed unclearly, informally or without citation (COM)?
Or is it how the task was handled (TST)?

codes.name: Literal Misread
codes.plain_name: Misread what happens in the text
codes.student_help: Reread the lines around your answer: who does what, to whom, and when?
codes.description: Gets the plain sense of a passage wrong: who did what, the order of events, or what a sentence states.
codes.example: 'In Act 1, Romeo is in love with Juliet' (he is pining for Rosaline).

tell_apart.how: If the student reads a figure of speech as fact, use CON_FIGURATIVE_AS_LITERAL.
If the answer comes from memory or general knowledge rather than the passage, use TST_TEXT_NOT_REREAD.

codes.remediation: Tier 1: who-what-when retelling of the passage.

codes.name: Figurative Read as Literal
codes.plain_name: Took figurative language literally
codes.student_help: Ask whether the words could really be true; if not, what are they comparing or suggesting?
codes.description: Reads metaphor, hyperbole, symbolism or idiom as literal statement.
codes.example: '"All the world's a stage" means the play is set in a theatre.'

tell_apart.how: If the student misses sarcasm or irony (the attitude), use CON_TONE_MISREAD.
If the student sees the figure but names the wrong device, use CON_DEVICE_MISIDENTIFIED.

codes.remediation: Tier 1: literal vs figurative sort with the effect of each.

codes.name: Tone Misread
codes.plain_name: Misjudged the tone or attitude
codes.student_help: Look at word choice: is the writer serious, mocking, angry, hopeful?
codes.description: Misjudges the speaker's or writer's attitude: takes sarcasm or irony as sincere, misses humour, or names a mood the text doesn't support.
codes.example: Reads Swift's 'A Modest Proposal' as a serious plan.

tell_apart.how: If it is a single figure of speech read literally, use CON_FIGURATIVE_AS_LITERAL.
If the student assumes the narrator's views are the author's, use CON_NARRATOR_AS_AUTHOR.

codes.remediation: Tier 1: tone-word ladder with evidence for each choice.

codes.name: Narrator Taken as Author
codes.plain_name: Treated the narrator as the author
codes.student_help: The narrator or speaker is a character the author created; their views may not be the author's.
codes.description: Treats the narrator, speaker or a character as the author, or takes an unreliable narrator at face value.
codes.example: 'Poe admits he is a murderer in "The Tell-Tale Heart".'

tell_apart.how: If the issue is the attitude of the text rather than who is speaking, use CON_TONE_MISREAD.

codes.name: Topic Given as Theme
codes.plain_name: Gave a topic, not a theme
codes.student_help: A theme is a full statement about life ("Ambition without limits destroys"), not one word ("ambition").
codes.description: Gives a topic word or a moral cliché as the theme instead of a statement the text makes about its topic.
codes.example: 'The theme of Macbeth is ambition.'

tell_apart.how: If the thesis of the whole essay is not arguable, use STR_NO_ARGUABLE_THESIS; this code is about naming a theme.

codes.remediation: Tier 1: topic → question → theme statement frame.

codes.name: Device Misidentified
codes.plain_name: Named the wrong literary device
codes.student_help: Check the definition: simile uses like/as, metaphor doesn't; irony is a gap between expected and actual.
codes.description: Names a literary, rhetorical or media device wrongly (simile for metaphor, irony for coincidence, foreshadowing for flashback).
codes.example: '"Her eyes were stars" is a simile.'

tell_apart.how: If the device is named correctly but its effect isn't explained, use PRC_DEVICE_SPOTTING.

codes.remediation: Tier 1: device definition cards with paired examples.

codes.name: Purpose or Audience Misread
codes.plain_name: Misread the text's purpose or audience
codes.student_help: Ask who the text is for and what it wants them to think or do.
codes.description: Misidentifies the purpose (inform, persuade, entertain) or intended audience of an informational, media or persuasive text.
codes.example: Calls a sponsored advertisement for a sports drink an objective health report.

tell_apart.how: If the student treats a claim as fact, use CON_FACT_VS_OPINION.

codes.name: Fact vs Opinion
codes.plain_name: Mixed up fact and opinion
codes.student_help: A fact can be checked; an opinion or claim needs support. Watch for loaded words.
codes.description: Treats opinion, claims or biased statements as facts, or misses bias in a source.
codes.example: 'The article proves that video games are a waste of time because the author says so.'

tell_apart.how: If the issue is the text's overall purpose, use CON_PURPOSE_AUDIENCE.

codes.remediation: Tier 1: fact / opinion / claim sort with loaded-word highlighting.

codes.name: Off the Prompt
codes.plain_name: Wrote about something other than the prompt
codes.student_help: Turn the prompt into a question and make sure your thesis answers it.
codes.description: The response or thesis addresses a different question or topic from the one set (writes about a character when asked about a theme, or a general opinion when asked about the text).
codes.example: Prompt: 'How does Shakespeare use the witches to build tension?' Essay: 'Macbeth is a tragic hero.'

tell_apart.how: If the prompt is answered but one of its parts is left out, use TST_SKIPPED_PART.
If the thesis answers the prompt but the body wanders away, use STR_THESIS_DRIFT.

codes.name: No Arguable Thesis
codes.plain_name: Thesis isn't something you can argue
codes.student_help: A thesis is a claim someone could disagree with, plus why.
codes.description: The thesis is a fact, a plot statement, an announcement ('In this essay I will...'), or is missing.
codes.example: 'In this essay I will talk about the symbols in Lord of the Flies.'

tell_apart.how: If the problem is naming a theme as a single word, use CON_THEME_AS_TOPIC.
If the thesis is arguable but answers a different question, use STR_OFF_PROMPT.

codes.remediation: Tier 2: claim + because + so-what thesis frame.

codes.name: Thesis Drift
codes.plain_name: Body moved away from the thesis
codes.student_help: Each paragraph's point should prove a part of your thesis.
codes.description: Body paragraphs argue something other than the thesis, or the conclusion reaches a different claim.
codes.example: Thesis about guilt; body paragraphs about Lady Macbeth's ambition with no link to guilt.

tell_apart.how: If a single paragraph mixes points, use STR_PARAGRAPH_FOCUS; this code is about the essay as a whole.

codes.name: Unfocused Paragraph
codes.plain_name: Paragraph has no single clear point
codes.student_help: Start each paragraph with one point; everything after should support it.
codes.description: A paragraph has no topic sentence, combines several unrelated points, or its point only appears at the end.
codes.example: One paragraph discusses setting, then a character's motive, then a quote about the ending.

tell_apart.how: If the paragraph is focused but off the thesis, use STR_THESIS_DRIFT.
If paragraphs are focused but not linked, use COM_WEAK_TRANSITIONS.

codes.name: Illogical Order
codes.plain_name: Ideas aren't in a logical order
codes.student_help: Put ideas in an order that builds: time order, weakest to strongest, or cause to effect.
codes.description: Ideas or paragraphs are ordered with no logic or progression; the argument jumps back and forth.
codes.example: Persuasive essay puts its strongest point first, a rebuttal in the middle, and a new reason in the conclusion.

tell_apart.how: If the order is sound but the links between ideas are missing, use COM_WEAK_TRANSITIONS.

codes.remediation: Tier 2: reverse outline of the draft.

codes.name: Overlapping Points
codes.plain_name: Points repeat each other
codes.student_help: Each body point should be a different reason, not the same reason in new words.
codes.description: The thesis or body points overlap, so the essay makes one point several times.
codes.example: Thesis: 'Jack is violent, aggressive and brutal.'

tell_apart.how: COM_REPETITION is about repeated words or sentence patterns; this code is about repeated ideas.

codes.remediation: Tier 2: point-distinctness check (can each stand alone?).

codes.name: Wrong Form
codes.plain_name: Used the wrong form for the task
codes.student_help: Check the form asked for (news report, letter, series of paragraphs) and its features.
codes.description: Writes in a form other than the one set, or misses its required features (a news report without a headline or 5Ws lead, a letter without salutation).
codes.example: OSSLT news report task answered as a personal story with no headline.

tell_apart.how: If the topic is wrong, use STR_OFF_PROMPT; this code is about the form.
If the form is right but far too short or long, use TST_LENGTH_MISMATCH.

codes.name: Weak Introduction or Conclusion
codes.plain_name: Introduction or conclusion is missing or weak
codes.student_help: Introduce the text, author and thesis; conclude by showing what the argument proved, without new points.
codes.description: Missing introduction or conclusion, an introduction without context or thesis, or a conclusion that only repeats or adds a new argument.
codes.example: Conclusion: 'In conclusion, that is why Macbeth is a tragedy. Also, Banquo is important.'

tell_apart.how: If the introduction is there but its thesis isn't arguable, use STR_NO_ARGUABLE_THESIS.

codes.remediation: Tier 2: intro funnel and conclusion so-what templates.

codes.name: Summary Instead of Analysis
codes.plain_name: Retold the story instead of analysing
codes.student_help: After each event you mention, explain why it matters to your point.
codes.description: Retells plot or paraphrases the text where analysis is asked for.
codes.example: Paragraph on the conch: retells each scene the conch appears in, with no claim about what it shows.

tell_apart.how: If there is a quote and a point but no link, use PRC_EVIDENCE_NOT_EXPLAINED; this code is for paragraphs that are mostly retelling.

codes.remediation: Tier 2: 'so what?' annotation after each sentence.

codes.name: No Evidence
codes.plain_name: Made a claim without evidence
codes.student_help: Back each point with a quote or specific detail from the text.
codes.description: Makes claims about a text without any quotation, specific reference or detail.
codes.example: 'Gatsby is lonely throughout the novel.' with no reference to the text.

tell_apart.how: If evidence is given but doesn't support the claim, use PRC_WEAK_EVIDENCE.

codes.remediation: Tier 2: evidence hunt with page references.

codes.name: Weak or Irrelevant Evidence
codes.plain_name: Quote doesn't support the point
codes.student_help: Choose the quote that proves your point most directly, not just one on the same topic.
codes.description: Uses a quotation or detail that does not support the claim, is too general, or supports a different point.
codes.example: Claim: Piggy is intelligent. Quote: 'Piggy wiped his glasses.'

tell_apart.how: If no evidence is given, use PRC_NO_EVIDENCE.
If the evidence is relevant but the claim reads too much into it, use PRC_OVERREACH.

codes.name: Dropped Quotation
codes.plain_name: Dropped a quote in without introducing it
codes.student_help: Lead into each quote with who says it and when, and blend it into your sentence.
codes.description: Inserts a quotation as a sentence on its own with no lead-in, context or grammatical integration.
codes.example: 'Macbeth is guilty. "Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood clean from my hand?"'

tell_apart.how: PRC_EVIDENCE_NOT_EXPLAINED is about what comes after the quote; this code is about how it is brought in.

codes.name: Evidence Not Explained
codes.plain_name: Didn't explain how the quote proves the point
codes.student_help: After a quote, explain which words matter and how they prove your point.
codes.description: Gives a relevant quotation and then moves on, or only restates it, without explaining how it supports the claim.
codes.example: 'Jack says "Kill the pig!" This shows he is violent.' and the paragraph ends.

tell_apart.how: If most of the paragraph retells plot, use PRC_SUMMARY_NOT_ANALYSIS.
If a device is named without its effect, use PRC_DEVICE_SPOTTING.

codes.remediation: Tier 2: zoom-in on key words in the quote.

codes.name: Device Spotting
codes.plain_name: Named a device without its effect
codes.student_help: Say what the device does: what does it make the reader feel, see or think?
codes.description: Identifies a literary or rhetorical device correctly but does not explain its effect or how it supports the argument.
codes.example: 'The author uses alliteration in "silent sea".' (nothing more).

tell_apart.how: If the device is named wrongly, use CON_DEVICE_MISIDENTIFIED.
PRC_EVIDENCE_NOT_EXPLAINED is for quotes left unexplained; this code is specifically for naming devices without effect.

codes.name: Overreaching Interpretation
codes.plain_name: Read more into the text than it supports
codes.student_help: Check that your interpretation fits the whole text, not just one line.
codes.description: Makes an interpretation the text cannot support or that other parts contradict.
codes.example: 'The green light proves Gatsby is secretly an alien.' / reading every colour as a symbol.

tell_apart.how: If the claim is reasonable but the quote chosen doesn't support it, use PRC_WEAK_EVIDENCE.
If the reading comes from misunderstanding what happens, use CON_LITERAL_MISREAD.

codes.remediation: Tier 2: 'what in the text supports and challenges this?' table.

codes.name: Counterargument Missing
codes.plain_name: Didn't deal with the other side
codes.student_help: In persuasive writing, name the strongest opposing view and answer it.
codes.description: Persuasive or argumentative writing ignores obvious opposing views, or only addresses a weak version of them.
codes.example: Argues for a four-day school week without addressing childcare or learning time.

tell_apart.how: If the writer's own points lack support, use PRC_NO_EVIDENCE.

codes.name: Run-on / Comma Splice
codes.plain_name: Joined sentences with only a comma (or nothing)
codes.student_help: Two complete sentences need a period, a semicolon, or a joining word like 'and' or 'because'.
codes.description: Joins independent clauses with only a comma or with no punctuation.
codes.example: 'Macbeth kills Duncan, he feels guilty right away.'

tell_apart.how: A fragment is a piece missing a subject or verb; a run-on is two sentences stuck together.
If slips like this are scattered through work where the student usually punctuates correctly, also consider TST_NOT_PROOFREAD.

codes.name: Sentence Fragment
codes.plain_name: Wrote an incomplete sentence
codes.student_help: Every sentence needs a subject and a verb and must make sense alone.
codes.description: Punctuates a phrase or dependent clause as a full sentence.
codes.example: 'Because he wanted to be king.'

tell_apart.how: If two complete sentences are joined wrongly, use FAC_RUN_ON.

codes.name: Agreement Error
codes.plain_name: Subject and verb (or pronoun) don't match
codes.student_help: Match singular with singular and plural with plural, even when words come between.
codes.description: Subject-verb or pronoun-antecedent agreement error.
codes.example: 'The group of boys are lost.' / 'Every student must bring their... his... they're book.'

tell_apart.how: If the verb's time changes rather than its number, use FAC_VERB_TENSE.

codes.name: Tense Shift
codes.plain_name: Switched verb tenses
codes.student_help: Write about literature in the present tense and keep it steady.
codes.description: Shifts between past and present without reason, or does not use the literary present when discussing a text.
codes.example: 'Gatsby throws parties and he wanted Daisy to come.'

tell_apart.how: If the verb doesn't match its subject's number, use FAC_AGREEMENT.

codes.name: Spelling / Homophone
codes.plain_name: Spelling or sound-alike word slip
codes.student_help: Check sound-alike words: their/there/they're, its/it's, affect/effect, then/than.
codes.description: Misspells a word or uses the wrong homophone.
codes.example: 'Its clear that there going to lose.'

tell_apart.how: If the word is spelled right but is the wrong word for the meaning, use COM_WORD_CHOICE.

codes.name: Punctuation Error
codes.plain_name: Punctuation used wrongly
codes.student_help: Apostrophes show ownership or missing letters, not plurals; check commas after introductory phrases.
codes.description: Misuses apostrophes, commas, semicolons, colons or quotation punctuation (other than run-ons).
codes.example: 'The boy's ran to the beach.' / 'However the plan fails.'

tell_apart.how: Comma splices and fused sentences are FAC_RUN_ON.
Punctuation of in-text citations belongs to COM_CITATION_FORMAT.

codes.name: Misplaced Modifier
codes.plain_name: A describing phrase is attached to the wrong word
codes.student_help: Put describing phrases right next to the word they describe.
codes.description: A dangling or misplaced modifier makes the sentence describe the wrong thing.
codes.example: 'Running to the boat, the conch fell from Ralph's hands.'

tell_apart.how: If the sentence is unclear for other reasons (length, wordiness), use COM_UNCLEAR_SENTENCES.

codes.name: Capitals and Titles
codes.plain_name: Capitals or title formatting slip
codes.student_help: Capitalise names and the main words of titles; italicise (or underline) long works and put short works in quotation marks.
codes.description: Misses capitals on proper nouns or sentence starts, or formats titles wrongly.
codes.example: 'in romeo and juliet, shakespeare...' / 'the poem Ozymandias'.

tell_apart.how: If the issue is the citation itself (author, page), use COM_CITATION_FORMAT.

codes.name: Unclear or Wordy Sentences
codes.plain_name: Sentences are hard to follow
codes.student_help: Say it in fewer words; one idea per sentence is fine.
codes.description: Sentences are so long, wordy or tangled that the meaning is hard to follow, though no single grammar rule is broken.
codes.example: 'The thing that the author is trying to show through the way that the character acts is that in a way he is not who he seems to be.'

tell_apart.how: If the problem is two sentences joined by a comma, use FAC_RUN_ON.
If one word is the problem, use COM_WORD_CHOICE.

codes.name: Informal Register
codes.plain_name: Too casual for the task
codes.student_help: In formal writing avoid slang, contractions and 'you'.
codes.description: Uses slang, contractions, text-speak, second person or a chatty tone where a formal register is expected.
codes.example: 'Macbeth is kinda sus and you can tell he's gonna snap.'

tell_apart.how: If the tone is wrong for the audience in a functional piece (a letter, a speech), use COM_AUDIENCE_TONE.
If the issue is 'I think' and 'I feel', use COM_HEDGED_CLAIMS.

codes.name: Imprecise Word Choice
codes.plain_name: Used a word that doesn't quite fit
codes.student_help: Choose the most exact word; if you used a thesaurus, check the word means what you need.
codes.description: Uses vague words (thing, stuff, good, bad) or words that don't mean what is intended, often from a thesaurus.
codes.example: 'The author utilises a plethora of imagery to make it more good.'

tell_apart.how: If the right word is spelled as a sound-alike, use FAC_SPELLING_HOMOPHONE.
If a specific literary term is replaced by an everyday word, use COM_IMPRECISE_TERMS.

codes.name: Imprecise Terms
codes.plain_name: Used an everyday word where a subject term was needed
codes.student_help: Use the exact subject word instead of an everyday one.
codes.description: The idea is right but is stated with everyday or loose words where a specific scientific term is needed, so the answer is ambiguous.
codes.example: 'In the paragraph of the poem' (stanza); 'the main guy' (protagonist).

tell_apart.how: COM_WORD_CHOICE is for general vocabulary; this code is for subject terms.

codes.name: Repetitive Wording
codes.plain_name: Repeated the same words or sentence pattern
codes.student_help: Vary how sentences start and use synonyms or pronouns for repeated nouns.
codes.description: Repeats the same words, phrases or sentence openings so the writing becomes monotonous.
codes.example: Five sentences in a row start with 'This shows that'.

tell_apart.how: If the same idea is repeated, use STR_OVERLAPPING_POINTS.

codes.name: Hedged Claims
codes.plain_name: Weakened claims with 'I think' or 'maybe'
codes.student_help: State your claim directly; your evidence does the persuading.
codes.description: Weakens claims with unnecessary hedging or first-person qualifiers in analytical writing.
codes.example: 'I think that maybe Piggy could possibly represent science, in my opinion.'

tell_apart.how: If the language is casual (slang, contractions), use COM_INFORMAL_REGISTER.

codes.name: Weak Transitions
codes.plain_name: Ideas aren't linked together
codes.student_help: Use linking words (however, as a result, similarly) and begin paragraphs by linking back.
codes.description: Sentences or paragraphs follow each other without transitions, so connections between ideas are unclear.
codes.example: Paragraph 2 starts 'Another thing is the setting.' with no link to paragraph 1.

tell_apart.how: If the ideas are in an illogical order, use STR_ILLOGICAL_ORDER; this code is for sound order without links.

codes.remediation: Tier 4: transition word bank by purpose.

codes.name: Citation Format
codes.plain_name: Quote or source cited incorrectly
codes.student_help: Cite with the format your teacher uses (for example MLA: (Golding 45)).
codes.description: Missing or wrongly formatted citations, page references or works cited entries; quotations not marked as quotations.
codes.example: Uses a sentence from the novel with no quotation marks or page number.

tell_apart.how: If only the title formatting is wrong, use FAC_CAPITALS_TITLES.
If the quote is cited but not introduced, use PRC_DROPPED_QUOTE.

codes.name: Tone Wrong for Audience
codes.plain_name: Tone doesn't suit the reader
codes.student_help: Ask who will read it (a principal, a newspaper, a friend) and adjust how you say things.
codes.description: In functional or persuasive writing, the tone does not suit the audience or purpose (rude, overly casual, overly emotional).
codes.example: Letter to the principal: 'Your rule is honestly the dumbest thing ever.'

tell_apart.how: COM_INFORMAL_REGISTER is about formal essay language; this code is about tone toward a specific reader.
If the student misreads the audience of a text they are reading, use CON_PURPOSE_AUDIENCE.

codes.name: Blank / Time Attrition
codes.plain_name: Left blank
codes.student_help: This part was left blank.
codes.description: Leaves a question or part with no attempt, from time pressure or a frustration block.
codes.example: Leaves the short-answer reading question blank.

tell_apart.how: If any work was started, use TST_ABANDONED_WORK.
If other parts of the same question are answered, use TST_SKIPPED_PART.

codes.remediation: Prerequisite baseline probe on that topic.

codes.name: Skipped Part
codes.plain_name: Part of the question skipped
codes.student_help: One part of the question was skipped while the others were answered.
codes.description: Answers some parts of a multi-part question and leaves another out, likely without noticing.
codes.example: Prompt asks for two examples and their effects; gives one example.

tell_apart.how: If the whole question is empty, use TST_BLANK.

codes.name: Tempting Wrong Option
codes.plain_name: Picked an answer that sounds right but isn't supported
codes.student_help: Check each option against the passage, not against what sounds true.
codes.description: In a multiple-choice reading question, picks an option that is true in general, uses words from the passage, or is half right, instead of the one the passage supports.
codes.example: Picks 'Bees are important to farming' (true in general) when the question asks what the passage's second paragraph argues.

tell_apart.how: If a written answer comes from memory instead of the passage, use TST_TEXT_NOT_REREAD; this code is for multiple-choice options.
If the student clearly misunderstood the passage, use CON_LITERAL_MISREAD.

codes.name: Abandoned Work
codes.plain_name: Gave up partway
codes.student_help: A good start was stopped or crossed out before reaching an answer.
codes.description: Starts a valid approach, then stops or crosses it out partway with no answer.
codes.example: Essay stops partway through the second body paragraph.

tell_apart.how: If nothing was written, use TST_BLANK.
If the piece is complete but far too short, use TST_LENGTH_MISMATCH.

codes.remediation: First-step confidence warm-up, then the same problem.

codes.name: Length Mismatch
codes.plain_name: Much too short or too long
codes.student_help: Check the length asked for (words, paragraphs, lines) and plan to fit it.
codes.description: Writes far less or far more than the task asks for (a paragraph for an essay, one sentence where a series of paragraphs is set).
codes.example: Series-of-paragraphs task answered in four lines.

tell_apart.how: If the writing stops mid-thought, use TST_ABANDONED_WORK.
If the form itself is wrong, use STR_WRONG_FORM.

codes.name: Answered Without the Text
codes.plain_name: Answered from memory, not the passage
codes.student_help: Go back to the passage and find the line that answers the question.
codes.description: Answers a reading question from memory, general knowledge or opinion instead of the passage provided.
codes.example: Reading question on a passage about bees answered with facts from a science class not in the passage.

tell_apart.how: If the student read the passage but understood it wrongly, use CON_LITERAL_MISREAD.

codes.remediation: Line-reference habit for every reading answer.

codes.name: Copied Prompt or Passage
codes.plain_name: Copied the question or passage instead of answering
codes.student_help: Use your own words; a quote should support your answer, not replace it.
codes.description: Restates the prompt or copies long stretches of the passage as the answer, with little or no response of the student's own.
codes.example: Answer to 'What is the main idea?' is the first three sentences of the passage copied out.

tell_apart.how: If the student paraphrases the plot in their own words, use PRC_SUMMARY_NOT_ANALYSIS.

codes.name: Not Proofread
codes.plain_name: Didn't reread for slips
codes.student_help: Leave two minutes to reread; read it as if someone else wrote it.
codes.description: A cluster of obvious slips (missing or doubled words, unfinished sentences) the student would likely catch on a reread, in work that otherwise shows they know the conventions.
codes.example: 'The the boys decide to to build a fire on the.'

tell_apart.how: Use the specific FAC code when a slip shows a real gap (consistent its/it's); use this one when slips look careless and scattered.
